lead: LPWAN stands for low-power wide-area network. It trades data rate for range and battery life: a small packet every few minutes can travel kilometres and run for years on one cell. Two common families are LoRaWAN, which uses unlicensed chirp radio, and NB-IoT, which uses licensed LTE spectrum. They serve water meters, gas meters, street lights, parking sensors and soil probes where Wi-Fi and BLE are too short and ordinary cellular is too costly.
prereq: You need: Chapter 3.2 on low-power radio and Chapter 3.4 on BLE for the short-range contrast.

blocks.text: LPWAN means low-power wide-area network. It is built for many devices that send tiny messages over kilometres and live on a battery for years. It accepts a low data rate, often 0.3 to 50 kbit/s, and a delay of seconds. The design goals are long range, low power, low cost per device and high capacity per gateway or cell. A water meter that reports one reading a day fits. A video camera does not.

items: Long range: several kilometres in a city and more in open land.
Low rate: a few bytes to a few hundred bytes per message.
Low power: years on one battery, so the radio sleeps most of the time.
High capacity: one gateway or cell serves thousands of nodes.

blocks.text: LoRa is the radio layer under LoRaWAN. It uses chirp spread spectrum: each symbol is a frequency sweep, called a chirp, across the channel. A receiver can decode chirps below the noise floor, so the link reaches far. The spreading factor SF sets how many chips one symbol uses. SF ranges from 7 to 12. Common bandwidths BW are 125, 250 and 500 kHz.

blocks.where: T<sub>s</sub> is symbol duration in seconds; SF is spreading factor (7 to 12); BW is bandwidth in hertz.

blocks.text: A higher SF gives a longer symbol. That adds range and lowers the data rate. It also increases time on air, so the node spends more energy and occupies the channel longer. The network chooses SF and power to balance these effects.

LoRaWAN is the network protocol above LoRa. An end device is the sensor node. A gateway listens on LoRa channels and forwards frames over IP. A network server handles join requests, removes duplicate frames from several gateways, runs adaptive data rate and routes data. An application server reads the sensor payload. Figure 3.7.1 shows the chain.

items: Class A: the default. After each uplink the device opens two short receive windows. It sleeps otherwise, so it uses the least power.
Class B: adds scheduled receive windows driven by a gateway beacon. It gives bounded downlink delay at extra power.
Class C: keeps the receiver open except while transmitting. It is for mains-powered nodes, not battery nodes.

blocks.text: ADR, adaptive data rate, lets the network server set the spreading factor and transmit power. A node near a gateway can use SF7. A distant node can use SF12. ADR saves battery and airtime.
The unlicensed band has a duty cycle limit, for example 1% in some sub-bands. After a transmission the node must wait. This limits how often it can send.

Join has two forms. OTAA, over-the-air activation, sends a join request with DevEUI, AppEUI and AppKey; the server returns session keys. ABP, activation by personalization, preloads the keys and skips the join exchange. OTAA is preferred for large deployments. ABP is simpler for a fixed test.

NB-IoT is a narrowband cellular standard from 3GPP Release 13. It uses licensed LTE spectrum, so the operator controls interference and can charge a subscription. The channel is 180 kHz wide, made of 12 subcarriers spaced 15 kHz. That is one LTE resource block. Some syllabi call this LTE Cat NB1.

items: Guard-band: uses unused edges of an LTE band.
In-band: uses resource blocks inside an LTE carrier.

blocks.text: Coverage enhancement, CE, repeats a message many times. A meter in a basement can reach a base station at high path loss. The cost is lower data rate and more energy per useful bit.

PSM, power saving mode, lets the device sleep deeply after a short active timer. It keeps its registration but cannot be paged. eDRX, extended discontinuous reception, stretches the paging cycle to minutes or hours. The device wakes less often and stays reachable. PSM saves more power; eDRX gives lower downlink delay.

The stack is cut down from LTE. PHY handles the 180 kHz radio. MAC schedules the shared channel. RLC and PDCP carry data with retransmission and ciphering. RRC controls the connection. NAS carries signalling between the device and the core network.
NB-IoT suits utility meters, smoke alarms, tracking and agricultural sensors where licensed spectrum and operator management matter.

figure.caption: One packet on a time axis: at SF9 and 125 kHz each symbol lasts 4.096 ms, so the 8 preamble symbols fill 32.768 ms and the 40 payload symbols fill 163.84 ms, giving 196.608 ms of air time in all.

spec.aria: Timeline of a LoRa packet at SF9 and 125 kHz: a preamble bar of 8 symbols runs from 0 to 32.768 ms, then a payload bar of 40 symbols runs from 32.768 to 196.608 ms, each symbol lasting 4.096 ms.

examples.question: A LoRaWAN node uses spreading factor SF9 and bandwidth 125 kHz. A packet has 8 preamble symbols and 40 payload symbols. What is the time on air in ms, ignoring other overhead?
examples.answer: The time on air is 196.608 ms, about 196.6 ms.
examples.check:
sf = 9
bw = 125000
preamble = 8
payload = 40
ts = (2 ** sf) / bw
ts_ms = ts * 1000
symbols = preamble + payload
toa_ms = symbols * ts_ms
print(ts_ms)
print(symbols)
print(toa_ms)

traps: LoRa is the physical radio layer; LoRaWAN is the network protocol above it. Do not use the names as synonyms.
NB-IoT is not a LoRa variant. It uses licensed LTE spectrum and a 180 kHz channel.
Class A is the default and has the lowest power. Class C keeps the receiver open and needs mains power.
A higher spreading factor gives longer time on air and lower data rate, not higher data rate.
PSM makes the device unreachable for paging; eDRX keeps it reachable at long paging cycles. Duty cycle is a regulatory limit, not a sleep mode.

quiz.q: What does LPWAN trade away to get long range and low power?
quiz.a: It trades data rate and delay: low bit rate and seconds of latency for kilometres of range and years of battery life.

quiz.q: Why does a higher spreading factor increase LoRa range?
quiz.a: A higher SF makes each symbol longer, so more energy carries each bit. The receiver can decode chirps below the noise floor. The cost is lower data rate and longer time on air.

quiz.q: A LoRa link uses SF10 and bandwidth 250 kHz. Find the symbol duration in ms.
One battery node uses Class A and sends every 10 minutes. Another node uses Class C and is mains powered. Compare their receiver behaviour and power use.
quiz.a: Class A opens two short receive windows after each uplink and sleeps otherwise, so it uses low power. Class C keeps the receiver open except while transmitting, so it has high power use and needs mains supply.

quiz.q: State the channel width and subcarrier spacing of NB-IoT.
quiz.a: NB-IoT uses a 180 kHz channel with 12 subcarriers spaced 15 kHz.

quiz.q: What does ADR do in LoRaWAN?
quiz.a: Adaptive data rate lets the network server adjust the node's spreading factor and transmit power. A strong link uses a low SF; a weak link uses a high SF.

quiz.q: Why does NB-IoT provide both PSM and eDRX?
quiz.a: PSM saves the most power by deep sleep but the device cannot be paged. eDRX uses long paging cycles so the device stays reachable with lower downlink delay. The choice depends on whether the application needs quick commands.

beyond: Not for the exam. Industry is adding firmware update over the air and roaming for LoRaWAN. NB-IoT is being folded into 5G massive machine-type communication. Researchers study energy harvesting for these nodes. Search for LoRaWAN FUOTA, NB-IoT PSM and 5G mMTC.
